name: Olga Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Days I do parcels in my old Skoda estate for one app, mostly the business park and the villages north of the river. From six till ten I switch to a scooter for takeaway in the old town, where cars can't get through the lanes. I've done the same pattern for five years, and I like that I know exactly where the stairs are.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work and the pay is good if you don't waste time. I've got the fastest runs because I know the back lanes. What wears me out is every app update, they move the buttons and I lose ten minutes figuring it out. My partner Tomas is an electrician, and he fixes things, so he laughs at me shouting at my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that talk for nothing. I wouldn't post, I don't really post. I'd say it at the depot over coffee and that would be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my two jobs and my routine, which suits me. We're saving for a house deposit, we've got about ten months of my pay put aside. Nothing changes, so the plan stays the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, parcels by day, scooter at night. I'd keep putting money in the deposit account every Friday. Maybe we'd look at houses next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nicely calm. I don't need the world to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the house you two are aiming for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small terrace near Tomas's mum, with a yard for his tools. Nothing fancy, two bedrooms. My partner Tomas and I have looked at the same three streets for a year, and I could drive them blindfolded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, maybe, and the scooter in winter when the lanes are icy. I came off once last January and missed two weeks. But that's the job, not AI.

say: I'd say all that **talk** was for nothing.
I'd say it at the **depot** over coffee, not online.
think: I keep my **two jobs** and my routine, which suits me fine.
The **house deposit** plan stays on track with ten months saved.
do: Carry on with **parcels** by day and **scooter** at night.
Pay into the **deposit account** every Friday.
S0.quote: My partner Tomas and I have looked at the same three streets for a year, and I could drive them blindfolded.
fieldNote: She values **routine** and knowing every back lane.
Her main risks are **physical**: her back and icy scooter runs.
The **house plan** with Tomas anchors everything.

steps.text: Keep the parcel and scooter shifts as they are
Pay into the house deposit account every Friday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see, it's not here yet. I'd tell people not to believe everything. Most of what they promise never shows up on my route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the app getting smarter, which I hate, but I can still drive. The robots are slow, so my parcels are fine for a while. The little takeaway robots can't climb the steps in the old town, so my evenings feel safe for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and if they force the new AI planner on me, I'd learn the bare minimum. I'd save a bit harder for the house, so we buy sooner rather than later. And I'd keep an eye on whether the parcel app starts dropping drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Like when a new manager starts and you don't know them yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at any other kind of driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for the council, bin lorries or the school bus. Tomas says council jobs are boring but safe. I quite like boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say his job is fine, robots can't rewire a house. And he's right. So it's me that's the risk at home.

say: I'd say **we'll see**, because it's not on my route yet.
I'd tell people **not to believe** everything the apps and news promise.
think: The app gets **smarter**, which I hate, but I can still drive.
Takeaway robots **can't climb** the old town steps, so evenings feel safe.
do: Learn only the **bare minimum** if the AI planner is forced on me.
**Save harder** to buy the house sooner.
Watch whether the parcel app starts **dropping drivers**.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a new manager has started.
S1.quote: The little takeaway robots can't climb the steps in the old town, so my evenings feel safe for now.
fieldNote: She sees herself as **the risk** at home, since her partner's trade is safer.
She'd consider **council driving** as a boring, safe option.

steps.text: Keep both delivery shifts and learn only forced app changes
Add extra each month to buy the house sooner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is mad and someone should slow it down. I'm not a march person, but I'd vote for whoever slows it. I'd tell my friends to stop spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking stuff passes me by, I don't do much thinking work, I drive. But robots by 2031, that's me finished as a driver. I'd be thirty-one with no other skills, and that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house hunt and keep the deposit in the bank, in case I need it to live on. I'd ask Tomas about becoming his apprentice, since electricians will be busy. And I'd keep driving every hour I can for the next four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest goes tight thinking about it. I don't like change at the best of times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd train with Tomas. Could you work with your partner every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, we'd probably fight about the van radio. But he's patient and I'm good with my hands. I'd rather be bossed around by Tomas (her partner) than by an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It waits. I'm not signing a mortgage on a job with four years left. Tomas would be disappointed, but he'd get it.

say: I'd say this is **mad** and someone should slow it down.
I'd vote for whoever **slows it down**.
think: The thinking side passes me by, but **robots by 2031** finish me as a driver.
At 31 with **no other skills**, that scares me.
do: Stop the **house hunt** and keep the deposit as a cushion.
Ask Tomas about becoming his **apprentice electrician**.
Drive **every hour** I can for four years.
feel: Dislikes **change** even at the best of times.
S2.quote: I'd rather be bossed around by Tomas (her partner) than by an app.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** matters, but she sees it ending her job outright.
She'd turn her **deposit into a cushion** and pause the house.
She'd retrain only through **someone she trusts**.

steps.text: Pause the house hunt and keep the deposit as backup
Start an electrician apprenticeship with Tomas
Vote for parties promising to slow robot rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's be sensible about it. I'd tell the drivers at the depot to start saving. I still wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2034, I'd be thirty-four. That's time to buy the house and pay a chunk off first. But I'd still need a new job, and I hate learning new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house this year, while I've got full pay. Then in two years I'd start the electrician course properly, evenings. I'd keep driving until the course is done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Better than the fast one, but it sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate learning new things. Would you really start the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, if Tomas signed me up and drove me there. I need a push. I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's an older lady on the parcel run, Gosia, who's been driving twenty years. She's got nothing else and she's not well. Gosia (an older driver at the depot) would be the one I'd worry about, not me.

say: I'd say we have a **few years**, so let's be sensible about it.
I'd tell the other depot drivers to **start saving** now, not later.
think: Robots around 2034 leave time to **buy the house** first.
I'd still need a **new job**, and I hate learning new things.
do: Buy the **house** this year on full pay.
Start the **electrician course** in two years.
Keep **driving** until the course is done.
feel: **Anxious**, but less than the fast one.
S3.quote: Gosia (an older driver at the depot) would be the one I'd worry about, not me.
fieldNote: She admits she needs a **push** to retrain.
With time she'd **buy the house** first.
She worries about an **older colleague** with poor health more than herself.

steps.text: Buy the terrace house this year on full pay
Start evening electrician classes in two years
Keep driving parcels and takeaway until qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, plenty of time, no need to panic. I'd tell people to get a trade while they're young. That's what my dad always said anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years plus three is me near forty. I'd want to be out of driving by then, so I'd have time. But I know me, I'd leave it late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house, settle in and keep driving. Maybe in five years I'd do the electrician course. Or I'd go for a council driving job and hope they're slow with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit of worry that I'd waste the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which way would you lean, the course or the council?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Council, if I'm honest. A council job is the closest thing to a job that never changes. That's what I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything else at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe have a kid sooner, while I've got good money. Tomas wants to. Ten years feels like enough room to do that first.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty of time, so there's no need to panic.
I'd tell young people to get **a trade**, like my dad always said.
think: Robots around 2039 put me **near forty**, so there's time to get out.
I know myself, and I'd **leave it late**.
do: Apply for a **council driving** job within five years.
feel: A bit worried I'd **waste** the time.
S4.quote: A council job is the closest thing to a job that never changes.
fieldNote: Even with time, she expects to **lose driving** eventually.
She'd pick a **council job** over retraining.
More time brings **family plans**, like a child, forward rather than back.

steps.text: Buy the house and settle in
Apply for council bus or bin lorry driving work
Keep doing both delivery shifts meanwhile

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. I'd have to change everything in a hurry, and I'm bad at hurry. What would help is a proper apprenticeship with pay, and the government not rushing robots onto the roads.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we're actually good at. People think delivery is just driving, but it's knowing which gate sticks and which grandad needs his parcel by the back door. A robot has to learn all that.

headlineQuote: People think delivery is just driving, but it's knowing which gate sticks and which grandad needs his parcel by the back door.
portrait: Olga is 27, does **parcels** in an old Skoda and takeaway on a **scooter** in the old town.
She and her partner Tomas, an **electrician**, are saving for a house deposit.
She's pragmatic and **resistant** to change, hating every app update.
She's calm in the plateau, but **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 since driving is all she knows.
With more time she'd buy the house and lean toward a **council job**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have to change everything in a **hurry**.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** and not rushing robots onto the roads.
